planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this Himalayan species is named for the strongly veined leaf surface and sets viable seed, unlike many sterile faassenii hybrids.

directions: The straight species grows taller and looser than compact selections like 'Blue Moon', sending up narrow, deeply veined green leaves and slim, densely packed spikes of violet-blue flowers from early summer into fall. Native to rocky slopes in the western Himalaya, it tolerates thin, mineral soils and winter wet better than most catmints once its roots are established. Shearing the whole plant back by a third after the first bloom flush keeps the habit tidy and triggers a strong second wave of flower spikes. Bumblebees and small native bees visit the spikes heavily throughout its long season.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; the fleshy tuberous roots rot quickly in winter wet, so a gritty or raised position is essential outside its native dry-summer range.

directions: Native to dry hillsides of Iberia and northwest Africa, this species stores water in fleshy tuberous roots and can go summer-dormant in extreme drought, re-emerging with autumn rain. Its grey-green, aromatic leaves are topped by short, broad spikes of pink-purple flowers held within noticeably showy, flushed bracts, giving a bolder color effect than most northern catmints. It suits rock gardens, raised beds, or Mediterranean-style plantings where winter drainage is sharp, but it is markedly less cold-hardy than Nepeta racemosa or x faassenii types. Established clumps need little supplemental water and resent rich, moisture-retentive soil.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or set divisions in spring, into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; this species tolerates heat and humidity better than most garden bee balms but needs good drainage through winter.

directions: This little-grown Mexican species carries narrow, aromatic, lance-shaped leaves and whorls of lavender-pink flowers with dark-flushed calyces atop upright stems through summer. It is best known as one of the two parents of the popular hybrid 'Peter's Purple', whose strong resistance to powdery mildew traces back to this species' tolerance for heat and humidity. Grown on its own it rewards sharp drainage and full sun with steady bloom that draws hummingbirds and bumblebees, and it holds up through dry spells far better than Monarda didyma selections. Divide congested clumps every few years to maintain airflow and vigor.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
